Selected exploratory associations within the sham group do not establish a difference between groups or a real-RF effect. The predominantly student sample, imperfect cover story and task-validity limitations constrain transfer to clinical symptoms.

Locator: Main PDF physical pages 5 to 7, exploratory analyses and Discussion. Basis: full text. Scientific review: pending.

Dummy-transmitter expectation manipulation, not a real-RF exposure trial. Exploratory associations, task validity and nonclinical sampling limit interpretation. Numerical release, scientific appraisal and human review remain pending.

Expectation instructions are the experimental contrast

The blinking repeaters were dummy equipment. The assigned difference was what volunteers were told about an enhanced electromagnetic field, together with the warning and laboratory story. This is a test of contextual expectations during perception tasks. It does not compare an actual transmitting router with sham, estimate absorbed RF dose or establish the effects of routine wireless-device use.

Do expectations shape interoceptive perceptions across body domains? A sham EMF study to test the predictive processing theory. Main PDF physical pages 2 to 3, Methods, procedure and cover story.

The expected group difference in response bias was not demonstrated in either bodily task. Exploratory within-group associations with symptoms remain distinct from that primary comparison, and a positive model in one group with a nonsignificant model in another does not itself establish a group interaction. The student sample, variable credibility of the threat story and task limitations leave clinical and causal interpretation open.

Rank agreement is different from identical readings

The meters were used simultaneously on selected walking routes, allowing paired comparisons within the bands common to the devices. The distributed meter was calibrated for each assistant, while commercial devices were affected differently by placement and shielding by the body. A similar ranking of environments can coexist with lower absolute readings or weaker agreement in particular bands.

Assistants were instructed not to use their own phones or electronic devices. The campaign therefore characterizes nearby sources under those route conditions rather than the user's own phone dose. Device failures, incomplete common-band coverage and crosstalk also remain relevant. A temperature endpoint under controlled conditions

Infrared skin-temperature measurements concern the surface regions observed during a brief controlled session. They do not measure every organ or physiological process. The authors identify the healthy young adult sample and controlled ambient conditions as limits on generalization. Their conclusion about this protocol does not directly validate an exposure-limit threshold or establish what happens during prolonged or repeated exposure.

No thermal skin effects at environmental 26 GHz field strengths relevant to 5G deployment.. Original PDF physical pages 10 to 11, limitations and Conclusion.

A small sample and the measurement interval could miss subtle or rapidly changing temperature responses. Children, older adults and people with altered thermoregulation were not established as covered populations. The unresolved difference between the pooled-result wording and its table also remains material: the source should not be summarized as every analysis being null. Convenience line-of-sight sites and limited control over active network bands constrain representativeness. Distance alone did not reliably predict the measured levels, and the campaign does not establish a universal distance rule or clinical health outcome.

Spot measurements and extrapolation answer different questions

Background readings, streaming and speed tests were taken under different traffic conditions, while the maximum scenario was extrapolated using stated resource and beam assumptions. The phone could switch technology or frequency band, and maximum loading was not always achieved. Those conditions matter when interpreting a comparison with a reference level; an extrapolated value is not an observed lifetime personal dose.

In‐Situ Measurements of Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields Measurements Around 5G Macro Base Stations in the UK. Main PDF physical pages 2 to 3, Methods; page 7, network-control limitations.

The locations were chosen for access and line of sight near urban and suburban base stations, without a rural sample. This limits population representativeness even when the measured values are below the reference levels used. Distance alone did not reliably predict the field, and the campaign followed no clinical health outcomes. Different distance-fit displays remain numerically unreconciled; neither a universal safe-distance rule nor a disease conclusion is established.

What this record contains

Source-checked statements

The induction-cooker study developed and validated an exposure-estimation model using household measurements. Distance from the hob centre was central to predicting magnetic-field exposure; wattage and cookware diameter also informed the models.

Locator: PDF physical pp2 to 3, Materials and Methods; pp10 to 11, Conclusions. Basis: full text. Scientific review: pending.

The model estimates instantaneous exposure at a fixed position. It does not capture movement, heat-output changes or cooking duration, and transfer outside Japanese homes requires validation. It does not itself estimate a health risk.

Locator: PDF physical p10, §4.5 Limitations; p11, Conclusions continuation. Basis: full text. Scientific review: pending.

What still needs review

Selected-passage extraction; complete scientific review pending. Kitajima induction exposure-model surveys; related Perinatal Cohort outcome reports require separate linking.

The source statements have not received human scientific sign-off or a formal certainty grade. The appraisal draft, where available below, records funding, overlap and correction checks together with remaining missingness. These checks have not received human adjudication. Report counts on this site are not counts of independent studies.

Integrity check: Validation concerns rank correlations, not individual dose agreement or health outcomes; preferred-model wording varies, so a unique superior model is not asserted..

An instantaneous model needs a time history

The model estimates a field at a fixed cooking position. Movement while cooking, heat-output adjustments and time spent at the cooker are separate inputs that the instantaneous estimate does not capture. A useful epidemiological exposure history would need that activity information as well. The model is specific to induction-cooker use, rather than a measurement of every intermediate-frequency source encountered during a day.

Measurement of Intermediate Frequency Magnetic Fields Generated by Household Induction Cookers for Epidemiological Studies and Development of an Exposure Estimation Model.. Original PDF physical pages 10 to 11, Limitations and Conclusions.

The household surveys and validation took place in Japan. Applying the model elsewhere requires checking the appliance and voltage conditions, body dimensions and counter geometry. The paper also describes difficulty obtaining appliance specifications from questionnaires. Validation of ordering or prediction within these surveys does not by itself establish an individual absorbed dose, a clinical outcome or one universally superior model.

Measurement of Intermediate Frequency Magnetic Fields Generated by Household Induction Cookers for Epidemiological Studies and Development of an Exposure Estimation Model.. Original PDF physical page 10, validation discussion and limitations; page 11, Conclusions.

SCIENTIFIC APPRAISAL DRAFT

What the appraisal adds

Human scientific review pending

This induction-cooker study developed an exposure-estimation method from household field measurements and a small validation sample. Predictions showed moderate rank correlations, which do not establish accurate individual or fetal dose. Fixed posture, clustered measurements and appliance differences limit generalisation, and model-preference wording needs clarification. The paper is useful for understanding exposure assessment, but it does not test pregnancy outcomes or demonstrate cooker-related health effects. Human scientific review remains pending.

What this record contains

Study scope. Swedish and Finnish COSMOS participants with baseline operator call records and later symptom questionnaires. Network-operator recorded call time, with network type and self-reported hands-free use considered.

Source-checked statements

The COSMOS symptom follow-up did not find an association between baseline call time and tinnitus or hearing loss. A small headache pattern weakened with confounder adjustment and did not follow a consistent call-time gradient.

Locator: PDF physical p11, Conclusions; pp9 to 10, Discussion. Basis: full text. Scientific review: pending.

Call records covered a short baseline window, and later outcomes were self-reported. Call time is an imperfect proxy for absorbed RF dose, and questionnaires at two time points cannot capture every symptom change.

Locator: PDF physical pp9 to 10, Exposure assessment and outcome-measurement discussion. Basis: full text. Scientific review: pending.

What still needs review

Selected-passage extraction; complete scientific review pending. COSMOS Sweden/Finland symptom follow-up; related to broader COSMOS cohort reports, not independent replication of the cohort.

The source statements have not received human scientific sign-off or a formal certainty grade. Integrity check: Printed tinnitus denominators and highest-category estimates differ between sections and Table 2; exact numerical summaries held pending clarification..

Recorded calls remain a proxy for dose

Operator records improve the measurement of calling behavior, but the baseline observation window does not describe every later call or operating condition. The symptom outcomes were collected by questionnaire at separated times. The authors discuss changes in use, participation and symptom reporting as limitations. A prospective design helps with temporal ordering while retaining those measurement and selection questions.

Headache, tinnitus and hearing loss in the international Cohort Study of Mobile Phone Use and Health (COSMOS) in Sweden and Finland.. Original PDF physical pages 9 to 10, Strengths and weaknesses.

The small headache pattern weakened with confounder adjustment and lacked a clear calling-time gradient. The network-specific pattern also did not align with a straightforward RF-dose explanation, and tinnitus and hearing loss were not associated with baseline call time. Lifestyle or other residual confounding remains possible. These findings do not turn call duration into a causal threshold or make related COSMOS reports independent participants.

Headache, tinnitus and hearing loss in the international Cohort Study of Mobile Phone Use and Health (COSMOS) in Sweden and Finland.. Original PDF physical pages 9 to 11, Discussion and Conclusions.

SCIENTIFIC APPRAISAL DRAFT

What the appraisal adds

Human scientific review pending

This prospective COSMOS analysis used operator call records and found no clear tinnitus gradient according to the authors; a weak headache pattern attenuated after adjustment. Exact tinnitus numbers remain held because printed counts and estimates conflict between the text and table. Short baseline records, self-reported symptoms and follow-up selection limit causal interpretation. The study does not establish effects of measured RF or sound dose, and human scientific review remains pending.

Glossary

RESEARCH GLOSSARY

EEG

Meaning, research examples and common interpretation mistakes.

Selected-source reading edition
Human review pending

PRIMARY INVESTIGATOR

Jonathan Pendergrass

EMF Shielding Engineer & Consultant

Contents
Context & save

Electroencephalography: a recording of electrical activity associated with the brain. An EEG change is not automatically a harmful effect.

Electrical activity is a measured endpoint

Electroencephalography records electrical activity associated with the brain. Researchers can analyze the recording for features such as frequency patterns during sleep. A measured feature has a particular scale and physiological interpretation; it is not a general score of brain health. Distinguishing the recording from the proposed clinical meaning is essential. A change can be scientifically interesting without establishing impaired sleep, a neurological diagnosis or a harmful effect on everyday functioning.[1]

The sleep-spindle result has a specific scope

The selected 5G experiment studied genotyped volunteers exposed to specified 700 MHz and 3.6 GHz signals before sleep. A shift in spindle center frequency after 3.6 GHz exposure was observed in one CACNA1C genotype group. That statement identifies a signal, EEG feature and subgroup. Replacing it with “5G damages sleep” would introduce a clinical outcome and a population-wide conclusion that the reported physiological observation does not establish.[1]

Separate signal frequency from EEG frequency

The gigahertz frequency describing an RF exposure and the frequency of an EEG feature describe different physical quantities in different systems. They should not be treated as a single frequency being directly read out by the brain recording. Interpretation also requires the exposure timing, sham comparison, analysis population and uncertainty. In this source record, the small sample and unresolved details about registry history and analysis prespecification limit how strongly the subgroup finding can be generalized.[1]

Analysis choices belong with the EEG finding

The sleep report distinguishes all-night recordings from the first sleep episode. Technical problems affected some whole-night recordings, while usable early-episode data were retained. A separate peak-selection issue led to exclusion of a participant from subsequent analysis. An EEG finding therefore belongs with its analysis population and recording interval; it should not be described as if every original recording contributed to every comparison.

5G exposure and sleep-spindle activity. Held repository PDF physical pages 6 and 8, EEG methods and spindle analysis.

The authors describe a genotype-dependent spindle-frequency shift and explicitly state that potential health effects cannot be concluded from it. Their spectral procedure selects the dominant peak and does not separately identify slow and fast spindles at the same channel. That physiological signal and its analysis choices do not establish a neurological diagnosis, a population-wide effect or a clinical sleep-harm threshold.
